orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, finishing her account to Lockwood in September 1802. She picks up a few days after the evening of Chapter XXXIII, in April 1802, when Heathcliff has begun avoiding the family at meals. Near the end the frame returns to the present, with Lockwood at the Heights that same September evening.

notes.g: A strong dislike of giving in.
Small apple trees, often trained against a sunny wall.
Evergreen trees; the stunted firs beside the house (see Chapter I).
The gun that burst and cut his arm (Chapter XXXII).

notes.t: shifted to that corner by the influence of Joseph’s complaints
notes.g: Moved there because of Joseph's fuss over his currant bushes (Chapter XXXIII).

notes.t: procure some primrose roots for a border
notes.g: Dig up some primrose plants for the edge of a flower bed.
notes.n: Primroses are pale yellow spring wildflowers.

notes.t: divine the occasion of his good humour
notes.g: Guess the cause of his good mood.
notes.m: 'Humour' means mood, not comedy. 'Divine' here is a verb: to guess.

notes.g: Sat down to the midday meal.
notes.m: Dinner was eaten at noon, not in the evening.

notes.g: Make up for not eating before.

notes.t: the inclination appeared to become suddenly extinct
notes.g: His appetite seemed to vanish all at once.
A low metal frame in front of the fireplace.
notes.n: It stops coals rolling out; plates could be kept warm on it.

notes.m: 'Thrill' first meant to pierce or vibrate, not to excite.

notes.n: In the north you 'get' a meal: you eat it.
He avoids even saying Cathy's name.

notes.g: Mere nosiness, with no good reason.
Close to the thing he longs for most.
notes.n: Keep in mind what Heathcliff told Nelly in Chapter XXIX about Catherine.

notes.t: hardly three feet to sever me
notes.g: Barely three feet separating me from it.
Sill of an open window with small leaded panes.

notes.n: A northern word from Old Norse.

notes.m: 'Ejaculation' meant any short burst of speech.

notes.g: The windows that open on side hinges.

notes.t: rattled some fire into the shovel
notes.g: Scooped burning coals into a shovel to carry to the other fire.
The room with the old oak box-bed, Catherine's childhood room.
notes.n: Lockwood slept there in Chapter III and dreamed of Catherine's ghost at its window. Heathcliff said in Chapter XXIX he could not bear to sleep in it.
A ghoul is a demon from Arabian tales that feeds on the dead; a vampire is a corpse that rises at night to drink blood.

notes.g: Looked after him as a small child.

notes.t: harboured by a good man to his bane
notes.g: Taken in by a good man, to that man's ruin.
notes.n: The good man is old Mr. Earnshaw, who brought Heathcliff home from Liverpool (Chapter IV). 'Bane' means the cause of ruin.

notes.g: Nelly pictures her own superstitious fears as a voice speaking to her.

notes.n: Where Heathcliff came from, and who his parents were, has never been known (Chapter IV).

notes.t: dictating an inscription for his monument
notes.g: Choosing the words to carve on his gravestone.
The church officer who digs graves and looks after the churchyard.
He had only the one name, Heathcliff.
notes.n: Old Mr. Earnshaw named him after a son who had died, and it served as both first name and surname (Chapter IV).
Drinks were often served in bowls in country houses.
A biblical phrase for the torment of the damned.

notes.m: 'Exquisite' meant acute or intense, here of pain as well as pleasure, not 'beautiful'.

notes.g: Doing what I begged him to.

notes.m: 'Speculation' here means looking or contemplation, not guessing or risky investment.
Not creative inspiration: literally, breathing in.

notes.g: Distract him from his dreamy trance.

notes.t: fell foul of the kitchen fire
notes.g: Set about the kitchen fire noisily.
The clock is striking four (in the morning).
Blow on the coals until they glow.
A hand tool that pumps air onto a fire to make it burn.

notes.m: 'Distraction' meant a frantic, half-mad state, not just losing focus.

notes.g: Mr. Green, the lawyer from Chapter XXVIII.
Kept alive by God long enough to repent.
notes.n: Christians believed you must repent of your sins before death to be saved.

notes.g: You would suffer a nervous illness.

notes.m: In British English 'knock up' meant to exhaust.
notes.n: The Titans were giants of Greek myth.

notes.t: look at yourself in a glass
notes.g: Look at yourself in a mirror.
notes.m: A 'glass' here is a mirror, not a drinking glass.

notes.t: from the time you were thirteen years old
notes.g: Since about the time old Mr. Earnshaw died.
notes.n: After that, Hindley sent away the curate who had taught Heathcliff (Chapter VI).

notes.g: A clergyman from any church or sect.
notes.n: Nelly doesn't mind whether Church of England, Methodist or other.
In Chapter XXIX Heathcliff told Nelly he had bribed the sexton to pull away one side of Catherine's coffin and of his own when he is buried beside her.

notes.g: He wants no clergyman and no funeral service.
notes.n: Very shocking at the time.
People thought to have killed themselves could be refused burial in consecrated ground.

notes.g: The dead don't simply cease to exist.
notes.n: A threat: he would come back to haunt her.
Said half mockingly.

notes.t: there is one who won’t shrink from my company
notes.n: He doesn't say who. Most readers take it as Catherine, whose presence he has felt for eighteen years (Chapter XXIX).

notes.g: Slide open the wooden panels of the box-bed (see Chapter III).
I fastened the window with its latch.

notes.s: Th’ divil’s harried off his soul
notes.tr: The devil's dragged off his soul, and he can have his carcass into the bargain, for all I care! Ugh! What a wicked one he looks, grinning at death!

notes.g: Dragged off; carried away by force.
Dead body (usually of an animal, so insulting).

notes.n: The same word as 'grinning', but with a fierce, snarling sense.

notes.g: Nelly's sharp name for pious Joseph.
Do a little dance of joy.

notes.t: the lawful master and the ancient stock were restored to their rights
notes.g: Hareton, the Earnshaw heir, and the old family line had got their property back.
notes.n: The Earnshaws had owned the Heights for centuries: remember 'Hareton Earnshaw' and '1500' carved over the door in Chapter I.

notes.g: Hareton lost his inheritance and his education because of Heathcliff.
Steel hardened by heating and cooling.

notes.t: perplexed to pronounce of what disorder
fearing it might lead to trouble
notes.g: Probably fearing it would look like suicide.
notes.n: That could mean an inquest and refusal of a churchyard burial.

notes.t: to the scandal of the whole neighbourhood
notes.g: Shocking everyone, since there was no minister and no service.
Made up all the people at the funeral.
Squares of turf, grass and roots together.

notes.n: Nelly stresses the word: country people say his spirit is not at rest.

notes.t: that old man by the kitchen fire

notes.n: Joseph doesn't say who the second ghost is.

notes.s: There’s Heathcliff and a woman yonder
notes.tr: There's Heathcliff and a woman over there, under the rocky bluff, and I daren't go past them.
notes.n: The boy doesn't name the woman.

notes.g: Under the nab: a jutting rock or knob of hillside.
The devil and all his armies of demons.
notes.n: A 'legion' was a Roman army unit; in the Bible a demon says 'My name is Legion: for we are many.'

notes.g: The stone slabs at the doorway.

notes.t: pressing a remembrance into the hand
notes.g: Slipping her a parting gift, probably money.

notes.n: Joseph already suspects Nelly of entertaining a 'follower' (Chapter XXXII).

notes.g: A gold coin worth one pound.
notes.n: A very generous tip, several weeks' wages for a farm servant.

notes.t: the three headstones on the slope next the moor
notes.g: The three graves together at the edge of the churchyard.
notes.n: Catherine was buried on a green slope by the moor wall (Chapter XVI), and Edgar beside her.

notes.g: Catherine's, the oldest grave, between her husband and Heathcliff.

notes.t: harmonized by the turf and moss
notes.g: Blended into the landscape by grass and moss.
Delicate pale-blue bell-shaped wildflowers of the moors.

notes.t: unquiet slumbers for the sleepers in that quiet earth
notes.g: Restless sleep for the dead buried there.
notes.n: The novel's famous last line. Remember that Lockwood himself saw a ghost at the Heights in Chapter III.
